items.title: The Highest Forms of Intelligence (None of Them Look Smart)
items.content_html:
Share

I’m embarrassed to say I never went to college.

I left high school 2 years before I was supposed to finish. I later tried to go back to school at 19 years old. The school principal thought I might have been a p3dophile and just wanted to return to hit on young girls (no joke).

I convinced them I wasn’t a predator. They let me back into school. And I graduated high school with terrible grades, right before I turned 20. Because of this, I’ve always had an insecurity around my own intelligence.

I’ve always secretly been annoyed at my lower than normal IQ. I thought it was a weakness. I even thought about going to university to get an MBA just to signal status / look smart and prove to the intellectuals that I can be at their level.

Over the last year my understanding of intelligence has totally changed. And I’m not the only one who got it wrong. Most people misunderstand what true intelligence is.

What intelligence isn’t:

  • High IQ

  • Sounding smart

  • Lots of credentials

  • A sense of superiority

  • Entitlement/privilege

  • Years of experience

  • Job titles

Here are the highest forms of intelligence I’ve seen firsthand in people who actually do sh*t and perform at the top of their field. (Warning: some are controversial.) Everything else is f*cking noise from fake-smart people.

1. Obsession

Many people are intelligent. They are smart on paper. They are book smart. But because they’re not obsessed, they don’t put all their theory and frameworks into practice. That leads to massive failure.

Obsession can’t be taught. It’s a way of life.

The word obsession secretly appears in every biography of every successful person in history. Just analyze David Senra’s Founders podcast episodes and you’ll repeatedly see the word obsession.

Passion isn’t enough. It’s lukewarm. It’s forgettable. It leads to a hobbyist mindset.

And it lacks intensity. So it doesn’t create outcomes. Many people get stuck for decades with their lukewarm passion and can’t understand what their roadblock is. I see it daily with people I interact with on Substack.

For years, I messed around being passionate. I was halfway into my banking career and halfway out. I wasn’t serious about romance either. I just wanted endless girlfriends. I dabbled with businesses too. One minute vending machines, next minute passive income digital products.

The moment I discovered obsession, everything changed.

It felt like I’d found god mode. Like nothing could stop me. Like there was no competition. This moment happened when a fellow writer got on a Zoom call with me. He spoke about my writing obsession.

Until he said I was obsessed with writing, I never thought about it that way. I realized he was right. My obsession with content wasn’t normal. It was crazy. It was relentless. It was high intensity and high reps. He said that was the secret to my success.

I’d never thought about it like that. He was right.

Nobody could match me on social media because I was obsessed like a psychopath. I had a level of intensity that scared people, and I didn’t sit there like an adult baby complaining about algorithms or low likes.

Obsession helps you transcend normality into a different layer of consciousness.

The intangibles it creates are hard to quantify, but at a base level it created better outcomes, intense aura, authority, and a perception of being a leader.

What Naval Ravikant says applies to obsession perfectly:

The only real test of intelligence is if you get what you want out of life.

2. Game theory

Smart people lose in life because they don’t understand the game they’re playing.

I did this too. I played the game without knowing the rules and got frustrated when things didn’t go my way. I tried to climb the corporate ladder the “right” way: keeping my head down, waiting for promotions, and racking up years of experience.

It didn’t work. People less smart than me rose faster. How?

They kissed ass and built a network.

They got opportunities because of who they knew, not because of skill. Game theory teaches you to understand the incentives of a game before you play it.

If you don’t, you’re guaranteed to lose.

So, when I learned this, I spent time having coffees with people and building my network. I got on the radar of people who could give me promotions.

Within a year, I went from a minimum-wage call center worker to being at Director level and helping Silicon Valley tech companies enter the Australian market.

This was a job everyone wanted.

Still to this day I look back and realize what an incredible opportunity it was. And I got it because of who I knew, not what I knew. That’s the power of game theory.

It goes deeper.

Once you truly understand everything in life is a game – careers, relationships, money, health – then you either become obsessed with the prize you get from winning the game, or the love of playing the game.

  • Amateurs are obsessed with prizes. They want the passive income so they can sit on the beach and jerk off to Onlyf*ns.

  • Masters fall in love with playing. They live to keep playing. They never want the game to end.

This ties back to obsession. Obsessed people love the game. You can be Novak Djokovic and win 102 elite tennis tournaments and still not want to quit. Because it’s not about winning. It’s about the love of the game.

A hater asked me the other day why I keep doing what I do online if I’m already a millionaire. I thought about it, then replied: “Money allows me to keep playing the game and to play the game at higher levels.”

You must practice the principles of game theory to be truly intelligent. Only a lab rat chases the cheese endlessly through a maze to get endless dopamine hits.

3. Pattern recognition

Every goal you want in life has a pattern.

True high intelligence isn’t going it alone with trial and error and relying on luck or hope. It’s not living a life of randomness either. No. It’s noticing the patterns and studying them.

This only works if you do an extreme number of reps. Otherwise, you’re drawing conclusions from a tiny data set and thinking you’re a freaking genius. Notice how I didn’t say watching passively on the sidelines or consuming more information?

Now you see why most people don’t see the patterns hiding in plain sight.

They never do enough (or any) reps to see the patterns. Or they do the reps, but they don’t proactively study the patterns the way an NFL coach studies game tapes after a big loss.

Seeing patterns isn’t enough, though.

True high intelligence is seeing the link between the patterns. Genius level is seeing patterns between different industries or totally unrelated ideas.

The best way to join the dots is by writing. That’s why writing a weekly newsletter is one of the best things you can ever do in life. It forces you to see patterns, and those patterns reveal deep wisdom.

4. Delusional optimism

Some days I can’t even log into social media.

There’s so much pessimism in the world. People have never been more fearful about problems that have existed for years.

And now AI has made people hallucinate. They think AI is going to replace everything because clever tech bros made them believe that. This is why having delusional optimism is an act of rebellion in modern culture.

True intelligence is understanding just how irrational the human mind is. It’s understanding the basics of human psychology, so your ape brain doesn’t scare you out of every good opportunity by mistaking a tiny insect for a lion.

Delusional optimism goes a step further. It’s optimism combined with self-belief, and I’ll-f*ck-around-and-figure-it-out energy.

Often there is no reason to be this delusional.

You just decide to do it because the alternative is low performance and psychological bankruptcy on every level (including financial).

When you’re not delusionally optimistic, you’ll give up easily. You’ll chase short-term goals. You’ll lack patience. And that means you won’t get what you want out of life which, as Naval Ravikant says, is low intelligence.

Doctor Brandon Luu shared a medical study that backs this up:

Delusional optimism is a secret to success.

People who overestimate their chances work harder and persist longer.

Even against the odds, that extra persistence turns failures into wins.

The willingness to back yourself and be delusionally optimistic produces outsized outcomes. And that’s the only intelligence that counts.

5. Admitting you’re wrong

Highly intelligent people are okay with looking stupid for years (even decades) to get what they want. And most of all, they’re not afraid to admit when they’re wrong.

In 1982, a c0cky investor named Ray Dalio was sure he’d figured out the future. He did what many financial gurus do and he pretended to be a fortune-teller or prophet.

Ray believed a debt crisis was about to wreck the global economy. And he didn’t just believe it quietly. He went on national TV. He wrote columns about it. Congress even asked him to testify.

Then Mexico defaulted on its debt, and for a moment Ray looked like a f*cking genius.

But the next great depression never came. The American Federal Reserve eased up. The stock market took off and kept going up. Ray was wrong. And everyone had watched him be wrong: on TV, in the papers, and in the Congressional record.

The consequences came fast. Real fast.

He lost his clients’ money, then his own. He laid off every employee at Bridgewater until it was just him alone in an office. He had to let his team go one by one until only he and one employee, Coleman, were left. Then Coleman had to go too.

He was so broke he had to borrow $4,000 from his dad to pay the family bills.

Most people would’ve protected their ego at this point. They’d say the timing was off, or the Fed got lucky, or they were “early, not wrong.”

Ray didn’t do that.

Years later he summed it up in 5 words: “I couldn’t have been more wrong.”

Then he asked a better question than “how do I prove I was right?” He asked: “How do I know I’m right?”

That question changed everything.

He stopped trying to be certain & started building a system that could survive him being wrong. He looked for the smartest people who disagreed with him & had them pick his ideas apart. He wrote down every painful mistake so he wouldn’t repeat it.

That system became Bridgewater, which grew into the largest hedge fund in the world.

Asked what he’d tell his younger self, Ray didn’t say “be smarter.” He said: “Why are you so stupidly arrogant!?!”

The smartest person in the room is rarely the one who’s always right. It’s the one who can say “I was wrong” out loud, in public, and then go fix it.

Your ego wants to be right. Your intelligence wants to get it right. They aren’t the same thing.

True intelligence is extreme humility. It’s the ability to be wrong and iterate fast. That’s how you produce uncommon outcomes and get what you want out of life. I pity the fool who thinks he is always right.

They are their own worst enemy. My old toxic micromanaging boss was like this. He thought his sh*t didn’t stink. He worshipped his own awesomeness. And now it’s left him unemployed.

Because people want to be led. But they don’t want to follow a knob head with a big ego who thinks they’re flawless. This is also why the influencer movement on social media died. We’re all sick of fake gurus and their polished success stories full of hidden lies and exaggeration.

We’re now in the AI era of authenticity. Time for everyone to show wins and losses, or risk being fake-smart.

Final Thought

Society has lost the plot.

We’re not worshipping true forms of intelligence. We’re being led by people who don’t get what they want out of life, who are trying to dictate how we should think and act.

It’s time you think for yourself. It’s time for you to use these odd forms of intelligence to produce uncommon results. Because people can argue about how smart you are, but they can’t argue with intelligence that produces real results.

People no longer respect scholarship or papers full of theory. People respect outcomes that produce change, heal pain, and make the world better. The good news it’s never been easier to join this movement.

You just have to focus on the right forms of intelligence.

P.S.

I’m sick and tired of all the “guru speak” everyone seems to be gobbling up today.

No, you CANNOT spin up a faceless Instagram account, have Claude write the posts, and casually bank $500K in a month.

Doesn’t work that way.

But there IS a reliable way to earn consistent revenue online.

Takes a little guts, and it’s definitely NOT for cowards.

I spill the details in today’s new video. Watch it now
